summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that gives a client a list of domain names or IPv6 addresses for SIP outbound proxy servers. It is one of several ways a SIP client can discover its local SIP server.

plainLanguage.summary: When you plug in a new phone, it needs to know which switchboard to call. This option lets the network tell it the switchboard's name or address automatically.

questions: how does a sip client find its outbound proxy with dhcpv6
what is the dhcpv6 sip servers option
how does a sip client find its outbound proxy
subtitle: Two DHCPv6 options that tell a SIP client which outbound proxy server to use, by name or by IPv6 address.

tldr.problem: A SIP client often has to send its requests through a local outbound proxy (for firewalls, local dialing plans or emergency services), but it has no automatic way to learn which one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two DHCPv6 options: one carries a list of domain names (option 21) and the other a list of IPv6 addresses (option 22), both in order of preference.
tldr.outcome: A client can learn its local SIP outbound proxy from DHCPv6, and should prefer the domain name list over the address list.

today: RFC 3319 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IPv4 counterpart is described in RFC 3361.

sections.title: Why SIP Clients Need a Local Server
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is an application-layer control protocol that can establish, modify and terminate multimedia sessions or calls. A SIP system has user agents, proxy servers, redirect servers and registrars.

A SIP client may contact the address in a SIP URL directly. In some circumstances it needs a local server for outbound requests instead: when firewalls are present, or when local dialing plans, local emergency services and other services have to be provided. Such a server is called an outbound proxy server.

This RFC defines two DHCPv6 options that let a client locate that server. The RFC says this is one of many possible solutions; manual configuration is another. The server named in the options MUST be an outbound proxy server as defined in RFC 3263.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a phone has to ask a local helper to pass its calls along, like handing letters to the school office instead of mailing them yourself. This document is about how the phone finds that helper.

sections.title: Two Options Instead of One
sections.content:
DHCPv6 has no shortage of option codes. The RFC therefore defines two separate options, one for domain names and one for IPv6 addresses, and avoids the encoding byte found in the IPv4 DHCP option for SIP servers (RFC 3361).

According to the RFC, this makes the option shorter and easier to parse, keeps the numeric addresses properly word aligned, and lets the client ask for either kind using the option request option. An implementation of the RFC MUST support both options.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one box where you must first say what kind of thing is inside, there are two boxes with clear labels: one holds names and one holds numbers.

sections.title: The Domain Name List Option
sections.content:
The OPTION_SIP_SERVER_D option has option code 21. After the option length comes a sequence of domain names, each encoded as labels in the format of RFC 1035: a one-octet length followed by that many octets, ending with a zero-length byte. A label is at most 63 octets and a whole name at most 255 octets. This encoding was chosen to accommodate future internationalized domain name mechanisms.

The option MAY hold several names, but these SHOULD refer to different NAPTR records, not different A records. The client MUST try them in the listed order, applying the mechanism in Section 4.1 of RFC 3263 to each. It only resolves a later name if contacting the first failed, yielded no common transport protocol, or named a domain that client policy prohibits. Names MUST be listed in order of preference.

Multiple names are not meant to replace NAPTR or SRV records. They let a single DHCP server point to outbound proxies run by several providers.
sections.plainLanguage: This box holds a list of names, best choice first. The phone tries the first name, and only moves to the next one if the first does not work out.

sections.title: The IPv6 Address List Option
sections.content: The OPTION_SIP_SERVER_A option has option code 22. It carries a list of IPv6 addresses of outbound proxy servers, listed in order of preference. Each address takes 128 bits, so the option length MUST be a multiple of 16 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: This box holds phone-number-style addresses instead of names, again with the best one first.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A client may request either or both options in an Options Request Option (ORO). If it receives both, it SHOULD use the domain name list. Only if no server in that list can be resolved or reached MAY it use the address list.

A server MAY send either or both options. If the client asks for both and the server is configured for both, the server MAY send only one, and SHOULD send the domain name list. A server configured with the address list MUST send it when the client requested the address list and not the domain name list in its ORO.

The RFC summarizes the server's response in a table, shown below.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone says which box it wants. The network usually gives the names box, but if the phone asked only for numbers, the network must give numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3315, RFC 3261 and RFC 3263 apply. If an adversary modifies the DHCP server's response or inserts its own, a SIP user agent could be led to contact a rogue SIP server, possibly one that intercepts call requests or denies service.

A modified DHCP answer could also leave out host names that translate to TLS-based SIP servers, which would make interception easier.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster slips the phone a fake switchboard address, the phone might call the trickster instead. That is the main danger.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned DHCPv6 option number 21 to the SIP Servers Domain Name List and option number 22 to the SIP Servers IPv6 Address List.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box got its own official number so everyone uses the same label for it.
